metadata.title: Web Security Fundamentals
metadata.description: Test your knowledge of common web security vulnerabilities and defenses.
metadata.author: security-team

questions.prompt: Which technique is most effective for preventing SQL injection attacks?

options.text: Using parameterized queries or prepared statements

questions.explanation: Parameterized queries separate SQL logic from data, making it impossible for user input to be interpreted as SQL code. Manual escaping is error-prone and parseInt only works for numeric inputs.

questions.prompt: Select ALL valid methods for preventing Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) attacks:
questions.explanation: XSS prevention requires a defense-in-depth approach: encode output, use CSP to restrict script sources, and validate/sanitize input. HTTPS protects data in transit but doesn't prevent XSS.

questions.prompt: What HTTP response header prevents a page from being embedded in an iframe (to defend against clickjacking)?
questions.explanation: X-Frame-Options (with DENY or SAMEORIGIN) or Content-Security-Policy with frame-ancestors directive prevents clickjacking by controlling iframe embedding.

questions.prompt: What is the primary security risk of storing passwords in plain text?

options.text: If the database is compromised, all passwords are immediately exposed

questions.explanation: Plain text passwords mean a single database breach exposes all user credentials. Passwords should be hashed with a strong algorithm like bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is the BEST defense against Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)?
questions.explanation: CSRF tokens are unique per-session values that attackers cannot predict. The server validates these tokens on state-changing requests to ensure the request originated from the legitimate site.
